steps.say: Some amputations are always being replanted. Thumb loss at any level, multiple digits, transmetacarpal patterns, any childhood amputation, and wrist or forearm levels are carrying absolute indications. Function regained is outweighing the operative burden in all of these.
steps.tx: Absolute indications for digital **replantation** (microsurgical reattachment of the amputated part) include **thumb amputations** at any level, **multiple digits**, **transmetacarpal** amputations (whole-hand level loss), any amputation in **pediatric** patients (children remodel brilliantly), and wrist or forearm amputations. These patterns always merit the attempt. These replantation indications admit no debate.

steps.say: Crushed and multilevel injuries are warning the surgeon off. Severe crush or avulsion, amputations at several levels, grave psychiatric illness, and warm ischaemia beyond six hours in muscle-bearing parts are standing as relative contraindications. Each factor is lowering the odds of a useful hand.
steps.tx: Relative **contraindications** (factors weighing against replantation) for replantation include severe **crush** or avulsion injuries, **multiple-level** amputations, severe psychiatric illness, and prolonged **warm ischemia** over **6 hours** in proximal amputations. Mangled vessels and dead muscle convert heroics into a stiff useless part. These replantation contraindications temper enthusiasm.

vis.alt: Crushed limb cascade with reperfusion hyperkalaemia, myoglobin kidney injury, and compartment syndrome.
vis.caption: Crush physiology with potassium and myoglobin release; crushed parts replant poorly. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Maximum tolerable **ischemia time** (the safe clock for the severed part) for digit replantation with **cold storage** (iced preservation) is up to **24 hours**, whereas **warm ischemia** (uncooled time) for proximal muscle-containing parts should not exceed **6 hours**. Digits carry no muscle; forearms die warm quickly.
steps.say: The clock is running differently for fingers and forearms. Cold-stored digits are tolerating up to twenty four hours of ischaemia. Warm muscle-containing parts are dying after six hours. Cooling fast is buying the finger a day.

The amputated part is surviving on correct packing. Saline-moistened sterile gauze is wrapping it, a waterproof bag is sealing it, and the bag is floating in an ice-water slurry. Direct ice contact is freezing tissue and is never being allowed.
steps.tx: **Amputated part** preservation (field handling deciding viability) wraps the part in **saline-moistened** sterile gauze, placed inside a waterproof plastic bag, floated in an **ice-water slurry** (melting ice bath keeping near freezing without frostbite). Dry ice, direct ice contact, and immersion in water all destroy tissue.

steps.say: Bone is giving the platform for everything delicate. Shortening with rigid skeletal fixation is coming first, then extensor and flexor tendon repairs, then the arterial anastomosis. Nerve repair and venous anastomosis are finishing the sequence.
steps.tx: Standard surgical **sequence** (the fixed replantation order) is: **bone shortening** and rigid skeletal **fixation** (stable platform first), **extensor** tendon repair, **flexor** tendon repair, digital arterial **anastomosis** (inflow restored), digital **nerve repair** (sensation reconnected), and **venous anastomosis** (outflow completed). Bone before vessels, inflow before outflow. This replantation sequence never varies.

The image numbers finger repairs from plate fixed **bone** through stitched extensor and flexor tendons to joined **artery**, then nerve and two veins. Bone gives the stable platform first, inflow comes before outflow, and **venous** drainage finishes the chain. Learn this fixed order because inflow before outflow protects the repair from congestion.
steps.say: The top panels show bone joined with a small plate, then the back tendon stitched, then the front tendon woven across. Lower panels show the artery joined under clips, then the nerve stitched, then two blue veins joined for outflow. Bone first gives a steady base. Tendons next, then inflow, then nerve, then outflow last, so blood can enter and leave safely.

vis.alt: Layered finger views numbered from bone fixation through tendons and artery to nerve and two veins in repair order.
vis.caption: Numbered finger repair from bone to veins, Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Veins are being repaired in duplicate. A vein-to-artery ratio of two to one is meaning two veins for every artery. Redundant outflow is keeping congestion away and is protecting the arterial repair.
steps.tx: **Vein-to-artery ratio** (outflow redundancy rule) of **2:1** means **two** veins repaired for every **one** artery, providing optimal venous outflow and minimising postoperative **venous congestion** (blood trapped by inadequate drainage). One vein alone invites the commonest failure mode. One vein alone invites the commonest failure mode, so a second vein is always sought even when dissection runs long.

**Hirudo medicinalis** (medicinal leeches applied to the congested digit) salvage congested replanted digits lacking venous repair by secreting the potent thrombin inhibitor **hirudin**, requiring **ciprofloxacin** prophylaxis (fluoroquinolone cover) against **Aeromonas hydrophila** (leech gut bacteria). Leeches drain until native veins open.
steps.say: Leeches are rescuing digits with no venous repair. Hirudo medicinalis is secreting hirudin while draining congested blood. Ciprofloxacin prophylaxis is covering Aeromonas from the leech gut until veins are taking over.

Fingertip zones are predicting difficulty. Zone one is lying distal to the lunula base and is needing supermicrosurgery on submillimetre vessels. Zone two is spanning lunula to DIP joint. Distal repairs are surviving less often than proximal work.
steps.tx: **Tamai classification** (fingertip amputation zones) divides digital amputations into **Zone I** distal to the **lunula** base of nail bed (the pale half-moon) and **Zone II** from lunula to **DIP** joint (the fingertip knuckle), with Zone I repairs reliant on microvascular **supermicrosurgery** (submillimetre vessel joins). Distal means harder.
